tip: English asks you TO read; Spanish can't. Asking someone else to act takes 'pedir que' + subjunctive: 'me pidió que le leyera' = asked that I read. No infinitive shortcut.
Where English says 'knowing', Spanish nouns the infinitive: 'el saber escuchar' = the to-know-how-to-listen. Never make an -ndo form the sentence subject.
Spaniards take your hair, not pull your leg: 'tomar el pelo' = tease someone. With 'me tomó el pelo' he 'took my hair', meaning he was only kidding about the lottery.
'De' + perfect infinitive ('haber sabido') is a formal, literary swap for 'si' + pluperfect: 'de haber sabido' = 'si hubiera sabido', had I known.
Future perfect guesses about the past: 'ya habrán llegado' = they must have arrived by now. It's speculation about a past event, not a real future.
Gave flowers? Not 'dio'. Spanish has a dedicated gift-giving verb, 'regalar': 'me regaló flores' = gave as a present. Plain 'dar' would sound like a mere handover.
'Esta semana' (this week) becomes 'esa semana' (that week) in reported speech, as the time-word shifts from now to then.
'Apetecer' runs backwards like 'gustar': the plan appeals TO you. '¿Te apetece que pidamos?' = does ordering appeal to you? And 'no me apetece cocinar' = cooking doesn't tempt me.
'Tendrá' doesn't mean he WILL be forty. Spanish uses the future to guess about right now: 'tendrá unos cuarenta años' = he must be about forty.
'Pase lo que pase' doubles the subjunctive: literally 'let happen what may happen'. That echo pattern is Spanish for 'no matter what'.
Thirty years in, Spanish still uses plain present: 'están casados desde hace treinta años', where 'desde hace' carries the whole 'have been...for' load, so no perfect tense is needed.
Comparisons take 'que': 'más satisfecho que el mes pasado', even when comparing times. The switch to 'de' comes before numbers ('más de cinco'); plain comparisons like this one keep 'que'.
No 'si' in sight: 'de' + infinitive packs a whole if-clause: 'de haber llegado antes' = 'si hubiéramos llegado antes', had we arrived earlier.
'Se me hinchó la pierna': the leg swells 'on me'. Spanish frames mishaps as happening TO you: 'me' marks the person affected, and 'la pierna' is the subject.
'Ser' for inherent quality ('viejo'), 'estar' for condition ('en buenas condiciones').
'Huelga decir que' = needless to say (very formal register).
'Cabe' + infinitive means it is fitting or worth doing: 'cabe señalar' = it is worth noting (formal register).
'Ser' for identity ('es médica' = she's a doctor), 'estar' for current state ('está de vacaciones' = she's on vacation). Same person, different info, so a different verb.
Tempted by 'realizar'? False friend: it means to carry out, not realize. Spanish 'gives itself account': 'se da cuenta de todo' = she notices everything.
'Los fines de semana': 'los' with a time word means every or on, e.g. 'los lunes' = on Mondays. Without 'los' it points to a specific one.
'Huelga' looks like 'strike', but it's the verb 'holgar' (to be idle): 'huelga decir' = saying it would be idle work, so it goes without saying.
'Tendría' here isn't 'would have'. The conditional is Spanish's way of guessing about the past, so 'tendría unos treinta años' = he was probably about thirty.
'Estar hasta las narices' pairs 'estar' with a set phrase for an emotional state, here fed up. Similar: 'estar harto/a' (to be fed up).
'Cuanto más..., más...' = the more..., the more...: 'cuanto más estudio, más me doy cuenta' = the more I study, the more I realize.
'Harina de otro costal', 'flour from another sack': sacks held different grades of flour, so another sack meant a different matter entirely.
What does 'las' point to in 'se las arregla'? Nothing. Some idioms carry a dummy feminine plural: 'arreglárselas' just means to cope. Stop hunting for the noun.
English needs 'the' twice in 'the further, the hotter'; Spanish uses none: 'cuanto más al sur íbamos, más calor hacía', where 'cuanto' opens the pair and bare 'más' answers.
'Don't give it more turns'? Spanish pictures worrying as spinning a thought: 'darle vueltas a algo' = mull it over, so 'no le des más vueltas' = let it go.
The system really does fail, yet 'falle' is subjunctive. After 'es raro que', Spanish marks your reaction to a fact, not the fact itself.
'Terminada la reunión' puts a past participle before its noun to mean 'once the meeting was over', a compact 'once X was done' setup.
